titleStmt.title: Ceiling Priority for Synchronous Communication in Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: Ceiling Priority for Synchronous Communication in Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Software complexity has increased in real-time systems such as automotive electronic control units (ECUs), as many functions are required for such systems. As software complexity has increased, component-based development has been broadly used to decouple software components for reusability, modifiability, and extensibility. Synchronous communication is frequently used between components in component-based development such as AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture (AUTOSAR). Previous studies on scheduling algorithms did not investigate the blocking and priority inversion problem in synchronous communication between tasks. We have observed that synchronous communication has same problem with resources sharing such as critical sections and semaphores, which have been investigated in many studies. The priority inversion also exists in synchronous communication between tasks since all consumer tasks communicating with the same provider tasks must wait until the provider tasks respond. We propose Ceiling Priority for Synchronous Communication (CPSC) for priority assignment and schedulability analysis based on rate-monotonic scheduling. The proposed algorithm was used for automotive battery management system (BMS) based on AUTOSAR and a multiprocessor in multi-criticality real-time systems.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: The priority inversion problem in synchronous communication between tasks affects schedulability and its analysis. A real-time system can hardly be designed without solving the priority inversion problem. Especially safety criticality systems require to conservative schedulability analysis. For many decades, real-time systems have been researched to solve several problems with various assumptions such as shared resource, aperiodic or sporadic tasks, and a multiprocessor. Specifically, we are concerned with fixed priority scheduling, blocking task, and priority inversion for safety criticality real-time systems, although safety criticality is beyond the scope of this paper. RM and deadline-monotonic (DM) are the optimal schedules in deadlines that are the same as the periods and deadlines that are less than the periods [1], [2]. The Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP), Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP), and Stack Resource Policy (SRP) have been researched to solve the shared resource problem between tasks [3], [4]. Methods to analyze schedulability more accurately were studied in [5]- [7]. Scheduling methods for aperiodic and sporadic tasks were studied in [8] and [9]. To address the shared resource problem in multiprocessors, the Multiprocessor Priority Ceiling Protocol (MPCP), Multiprocessor Stack Resource Policy (MSRP), Flexible Multiprocessor Locking Protocol (FMLP), Optimal Locking Protocol (OMLP), and Multiprocessor Resource Sharing Protocol (MRSP) were studied in [10]- [14]. However, to our knowledge, no existing research has solved the priority inversion problem in synchronous communication between tasks. Synchronous communication is widely used in component-based development (CBD) such as AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture (AUTOSAR). CBD offers the benefit of decoupling software components (SWCs) for modifiability, reusability, and extensibility to reduce development costs and schedules. In AUTOSAR, SWCs consist of one or more runnables that are mapped to the tasks for scheduling. If two SWCs connected through a client-server (CS) port and each runnable is mapped to different tasks, the tasks communicate via CS, as one is the server and the other is the client. In synchronous CS communication, client tasks wait for server tasks to respond. We used rate-monotonic scheduling based on AUTOSAR and a multiprocessor in a multi-criticality real-time system. We solved the multiprocessor locking problem with software architecture design instead of multiprocessor locking protocols. At the initial stage of the project, we implemented a sporadic server for server tasks by measuring the running time of the sporadic server and the event between the sporadic server and a real-time measurement (RTM) idle task. However, we did not proceed with it although it was implemented with small code changes since the AUTOSAR platform was supplied by a third party. Also, we would have to make a considerable effort for safety certification once we modified the single code provided by the third party. Another reason is that a multicriticality system requires functions to be mapped to different tasks as safety critical level. Thus, several jobs served by one sporadic server is not possible in a multi-criticality system. To meet the requirement of a multi-criticality system, we would have to instantiate several sporadic servers as safety critical level, which would increase complexity and decrease modifiability. Finally, we decided to design and use Ceiling Priority for Synchronous Communication (CPSC) to solve the priority inversion and blocking problems with schedulability analysis. In our project, we did not use shared resources at all since each shared resource was mapped to a different server task. We expect that shared resources will be replaced with server tasks in CBD and multi-criticality systems. The AUTOSAR platform will be useful in clarifying scheduling problems in synchronous communication between tasks. The platform is the prevalent solution for automotive electronic control systems (ECUs). However, CPSC will not be limited in AUTOSAR since one task blocking another is always a problem in synchronous communication, whether it is CS or event-based communication.

In this study, we investigated the priority assignment problem in synchronous communication between tasks for automotive battery management system (BMS). Section II of this paper presents synchronous communication based on AUTOSAR and the priority inversion problem. Section III proposes a CPSC (Ceiling Priority for Synchronous Communication) algorithm to solve the priority inversion problem. Section IV analyzes schedulability in a ratemonotonic scheduling algorithm with CPSC. Section V presents a practical case with CPSC and schedulability analysis. It also recommends a design method to create tasks as project environments. Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: A. Synchronous Communication.
div.p: CS communication is frequently used between SWCs to read and write physical data. This section identifies scheduling problems and shows the original PCP, which cannot be used for synchronous communication between tasks. Fig. 1 shows one of the designs in which two client SWCs communicate with one server SWC. Iohw_Cttr SWC includes a runnable to control digital output, which is peripheral as a single resource that must be protected by a critical section to prevent reentrancy if the "canBeInvokeConcurrently" option is enabled. We can minimize the blocking time with an optimized critical section if the server tasks can be invoked concurrently. ActCttr and CurrSnsr are conntected to Iohw_Cttr via the CS interface in component view. The runnables in ActCttr and CurrSnsr SWCs have a period, but the runnable in Iohw_Cttr does not. If all runnables are mapped to the same task, then the problem is exactly the same as the resource problem, which can be solved with the PCP since the ActCttr and CurrSnsr runnables will directly call the CurrSnsr runnable. However, if the runnables in ActCttr and CurrSnsr are mapped to different tasks from the runnable mapped in Iohw_Cttr, then the PCP can no longer provide a solution since the resource priority will be compared to the priority of the task with the Iohw_Cttr runnable. All SWCs are instantiated in Fig. 2. The runnables must be mapped to the task for scheduling. The task must be mapped to the application. In a multi-criticality system, there are several applications with memory partitioning as safety critical level. In a more practical case, one SWC can have several runnables, which can be mapped to different tasks as a period or safety criticality level. Also, several tasks are mapped to the application as a safety critical level. However, the problem is the same, whether tasks are in the same or in different applications.

div.head: B. The Priority Inversion Problem in Synchronous
div.p: Communication Between Tasks.

We observed the priority inversion problem when we designed the scheduling policy for a real-time system in AUTOSAR in a battery management system (BMS). Priority inversion affects schedulability in the rate-monotonic scheduling algorithm. In our investigation, the priority inversion phenomenon was the same as in resource sharing. Suppose that T1, T2, and T3 are three tasks. T1 has the highest priority, and T3 has the lowest. T1 requests T3 to execute a function and then waits for a response from T3. While T3 executes, T2 preempts T3. Thus, T1 is indirectly preempted by the medium-priority task T2. This example illustrates that there is exactly the same problem in priority inversion as in shared resources in [3]. Although there are no resources in this example, we still see the priority inversion problem in synchronous communication. There are two methods for synchronous communication in AUTOSAR: a server task is set to a basic task (Fig. 3), or a server task is set to an extended task (Fig. 4). The runtime environment (RTE) activates the T3 task when it is requested by T1 (Fig. 3). The T3 task state is changed from SUSPEND to RUNNING. T1 is in the WAIT state, awaiting response from T3. The RTE will set the event to T1 again when it receives the result from T3. In Fig. 4, the RTE sets the event to T3 when it is requested by T1. The T3 task state switches from WAIT to RUNNING. Priority inversion, whereby a medium-priority task indirectly preempts T1, can occur in both an extended server task (EST) and a basic server task (BST). We created the ESTs to dispatch periodic runnables, as well as server runnables. We created the BSTs to dispatch server runnables. Periodic runnables mixed with server runnables in the same task increase the complexity of schedulability analysis because the task has only one priority and becomes a sporadic or aperiodic task. Therefore, we mapped periodic and server runnables to different tasks.

div.head: III. CEILING PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT IN SYNCHRONOUS COMMUNICATION BETWEEN TASKS
div.p: Priority inversion affects real-time performance and schedulability analysis. A safety criticality or mixed criticality system is required to provide evidence or rationale of schedulability as ISO 26262 for automotive ECUs. Many realtime systems in automotive ECUs are safety criticality or mixed criticality systems. We designed CPSC to solve the priority inversion problem and enable schedulability analysis. The basic idea of CPSC (ceiling priority in synchronized communication between tasks) is to assign the highest priority among the consumer tasks to the provider task. All tasks with a fixed priority based on RM can communicate with other tasks synchronously or asynchronously. Same-priority tasks are serviced as first in, first out (FIFO). Definition 1. An asynchronous periodic task will asynchronously communicate with other tasks or will not communicate with other tasks. In AUTOSAR, the tasks using sender-receiver (SR) or asynchronous CS communication can be asynchronous periodic tasks. A set of asynchronous periodic tasks is 𝑡 𝑎 = {𝑡 1 𝑎 , … , 𝑡 𝑛 𝑎 }.

Definition 2. A consumer periodic task having a periodic task property invokes one or more provider tasks and is blocked until receiving a response from a provider or hybrid task. In AUTOSAR, client tasks can be consumer periodic tasks in CS communication. A set of consumer tasks is 𝑡 𝑐 = {𝑡 1 𝑐 , … , 𝑡 𝑛 𝑐 }.

div.head: Definition 3.
div.p: A provider task having a sporadic task property is invoked by a hybrid or consumer task. In AUTOSAR, server tasks can be provider tasks in CS communication. A set of provider tasks before being assigned a priority is 𝑣 = {𝑣 1 , … , 𝑣 𝑛 }. Definition 4. A hybrid task having a consumer task and a provider task property invokes a provider task and is invoked by a consumer task. In AUTOSAR, a task can be a hybrid task if both the server and the client runnables are mapped to the task. A set of hybrid tasks before being assigned a priority is ℎ = {ℎ 1 , … , ℎ 𝑛 }.

Suppose a tasks execution time as follows: In our project, 𝑣 and ℎ tasks were created for device drivers as Iohw or complex device drivers (CDDs) in AUTOSAR. At the beginning of the project, we created ℎ tasks to abstract and divide CDD functions into several Iohws. Application software (ASW) was connected to Iohw through the CS interface instead of CDD, and Iohw was connected to CDD through the CS interface. As (8), (9), and (10), we can expect that dividing single CDD into several Iohws increases schedulability with small blocking times since a single function of 𝑣 is divided into several small functions to ℎ tasks. However, this causes an increase in CPU utilization because of the additional execution time of ℎ tasks, as well as context switching overhead. Also, the design requires additional work to modify most of the code in ℎ tasks whenever a CDD is changed. There are no advantages to adding ℎ tasks if CDDs are frequently changed for reasons such as ongoing semiconductor development and hardware or system changes. Given the context switching overhead and the increased cost, we recommend minimizing ℎ tasks.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we showed that synchronous communication between tasks has the same problems as resource sharing. We showed the blocking problem in synchronous communication between tasks with fixed priority scheduling for real-time systems developed by CBD. We solved the priority assignment problem for asynchronous, consumer, hybrid, and provider tasks with CPSC, which is based on the same idea as the PCP. Also, we derived sufficient conditions for tasks designed by CPSC. Finally, we presented a practical case of CPSC and schedulability analysis.
